newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - No payrolls panic?.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - No payrolls panic?.

text.p: Could a month ever pass when investors weren't whipped into a frenzy, fretting over the monthly U.S. jobs report?
Well, October could be that month.
Of course, September's employment report will be the standout economic release for credit markets next week.
But expectations for below-average jobs growth, tame wages and an uptick in the unemployment rate should hold the monthly jobs hubbub to a dull roar.
The jobs report is always crucial for financial markets, given the look it provides into the strength of the economy and the potential thinking of Federal Reserve policy makers.

However, forecasts for payrolls growth of 166,000, an unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, and a 0.2-percent rise in average hourly earnings, won't be enough to shake prices of Treasury securities, let alone central bankers, experts said.

"This is the type of report that would be easily tolerated by people in the market and would not lead anyone to expect the Fed to tighten monetary policy soon," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Moran estimated 175,000 new jobs were created in the month; the jobless rate rose 0.1 percentage point, and average hourly earnings gained 0.3 percent.
The Labor Department will release September jobs data on Friday, October 4 at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

Following the Federal Reserve's decision earlier this week to hold short-term interest rates steady, market players are anxious to know what -- if anything -- might push the central bank to hike rates before its next confab on November 13.

"You'd have to see payrolls above 250,000, the jobless rate down a tenth to 5.0 percent, and earnings (up) three tenths or above," said Moran. "If we get a jobless rate of 5.0 percent, (Fed policy markers) are going to be very nervous."
Economists at the Conference Board, a New York-based business research organization, predict the unemployment rate will slip below 5.0 percent as early as the first quarter of next year.
In August, the economy added 250,000 new jobs, and the unemployment rate fell to 5.1 percent, its lowest in more than seven years. Earnings rose six cents to $11.87 an hour.

Adding to sentiment September jobs could be a non-event is the fact that Fed officials will have the benefit of yet another payrolls report before their next Fed policy meeting on November 13, pundits pointed out.
October jobs data, they said, could alter the employment picture, but for the near-term, the labor market remains calm.

"The (Treasury) market is positioning itself for a favorable headline number from the (September) jobs report," said Cary Leahey, vice president and senior financial market economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.

Job creation "looks like it will be 100,000 below trend, at around 175,000. With that, you could start building a case that ... the Fed finds the (economic) temperature of the porridge just about perfect," Leahey added.

In addition to September payrolls, the Treasury market will witness this month's index of manufacturing activity from the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) on Tuesday, and new home sales the day before.
Experts forecast a 52.5 reading on the NAPM and an annualized rate of 744,000 new homes sold in the month.

Economists had talked about a slightly higher reading on NAPM for September, but said a sharp drop in August durable goods orders released Thursday shook their confidence in their initial predictions.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1661
